readme.html:
What this module covers

This module explains how cloud security is shared between AWS and its customers, starting with authentication, authorization and the AWS shared responsibility model. It then walks through three groups of AWS security controls: preventing unauthorized access with AWS IAM and related services, protecting networks, applications and data, and detecting and responding to incidents. It closes with places to find AWS security documentation and third-party security tools on AWS Marketplace.

readme.html:
Lessons

Module 9 Introduction

  1. Introduction to Security on AWS: authentication versus authorization, the shared responsibility model and the three groups of AWS security controls.

AWS Security Controls

  1. Preventing Unauthorized Access: the root user and MFA, IAM users, groups, roles and policies, least privilege, an IAM console demo, IAM Identity Center, Secrets Manager and Systems Manager.
  2. Protecting Networks and Applications: DoS and DDoS attacks, the UDP flood, security groups, ELB, Regions, AWS Shield and AWS WAF.
  3. Protecting Data: encryption at rest and in transit, built-in encryption in S3, EBS and DynamoDB, AWS KMS, ACM and Amazon Macie.
  4. Detecting and Responding to Security Incidents: Amazon Inspector, Amazon GuardDuty, Amazon Detective and AWS Security Hub.
  5. Additional Security Resources: AWS security documentation sources and security tools on AWS Marketplace.

readme.title: Key takeaways
readme.html:
Key takeaways

  • Authentication verifies identity, and authorization decides what that identity may do.
  • AWS secures the cloud itself (software, virtualization, hardware, global infrastructure and physical data centers), while customers secure what they put in it (data, workloads, service choices and access).
  • AWS supplies security tools such as encryption and IAM, and customers are responsible for configuring and using them.
  • Lock down the AWS account root user with a strong password and MFA, and use IAM identities for daily work.
  • IAM denies everything by default, and the principle of least privilege guides what you then allow.
  • IAM users are individuals, groups share permissions, roles grant temporary permissions, and JSON policies define access once attached to an identity.
  • IAM Identity Center gives the workforce single sign-on through federation, Secrets Manager centrally stores, retrieves and rotates credentials and API keys, and Systems Manager oversees and patches nodes.
  • Region-scale infrastructure, customer-configured security groups and Elastic Load Balancing absorb DDoS traffic, AWS Shield Standard is free and Shield Advanced is paid, and AWS WAF blocks requests from IP addresses on a web ACL.
  • Data is protected at rest by built-in encryption and AWS KMS keys and in transit by SSL/TLS certificates managed in ACM, while Amazon Macie finds sensitive data in S3.
  • Amazon Inspector finds vulnerabilities, GuardDuty detects threats, Detective investigates root causes, and Security Hub aggregates findings.

readme.title: Summary
readme.html:
Summary

  • Security on AWS is a partnership: AWS guards the infrastructure, and each customer guards what they build on it.
  • Prevent: control who can act with IAM, a locked-down root user and least privilege.
  • Protect: rely on Region-scale infrastructure, AWS Shield and AWS WAF for networks and apps, and on encryption with AWS KMS and ACM for data.
  • Detect and respond: find, investigate and track problems with Amazon Inspector, Amazon GuardDuty, Amazon Detective and AWS Security Hub.

Introduction to Security on AWS

Objectives

  • Tell from .
  • Split security duties by owner.
  • Name the three AWS control goals.

Notes

Authentication and authorization

  • Authentication checks credentials, like a username and password, to prove identity.
  • Authorization then uses granted rights to limit that identity's actions.
  • Example: a portal login is authentication, and seeing only your own file is authorization.
  • Encryption (encoding data) and auditing (reviewing logs) are separate.
  • Both guard users' personal data, keeping trust and blocking identity theft, fraud and misuse.

Shared responsibility

  • Customer side: .
    • Customers control their content, so they secure all they create and manage: data, systems, apps, access.
    • They pick what data and workloads to store or run, and on which services.
  • AWS side: .
    • AWS runs every layer: service software, virtualization, hardware, Regions, AZs, edge locations.
    • Physical sites too: building access, environmental safeguards, redundant power and surveillance.
  • AWS supplies tools such as encryption and , and customers configure them.

Security controls

  • Controls prevent incidents by access management, protect networks, apps and data, and detect and respond to incidents.

Visuals

  • Key concepts timeline: portal example, shared model, control goals.

Key takeaways

  • Authentication proves identity, then authorization limits actions.
  • Customers secure data, workloads, service choices and access.
  • AWS secures the infrastructure and physical sites.
  • Controls: prevent, protect, detect and respond.

Scenarios

  • A signed-in user's request is checked against their rights: authorization.
  • Sensitive records on AWS: the customer protects them.

Terms

  • Authentication: Proving identity with credentials.
  • Authorization: Deciding what a proven identity may do.
  • AWS Shared Responsibility Model: The AWS-customer security split.
  • Security in the cloud: The customer's share of security duties.
  • Security of the cloud: The AWS share of security duties.

preventing-unauthorized-access.html:
Preventing Unauthorized Access

Objectives

  • Explain why is the first defense against unauthorized access.
  • Secure the root user as AWS advises.
  • Choose the right IAM identity and policy for an access need.
  • Match IAM Identity Center, Secrets Manager and Systems Manager to their jobs.

Notes

The AWS account root user

  • Every new AWS account comes with a root user, the owner, who can do anything and cannot be restricted.
  • : the owner can work the register, the stock system or anything else in the shop.
  • Give it a strong password and turn on right after the first root login.
  • MFA requires at least two kinds of proof, such as the password plus a one-time code from a phone app.
  • Even then, keep the root user out of daily work and use IAM identities instead.
  • Exam guide update verified 2026-10-09, Set an account password policy for IAM users Password policies set account-wide rules for passwords, such as minimum length, required character types, expiration and preventing reuse, but they never apply to the root user password.

IAM, default deny and least privilege

  • AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) gives fine-grained control over identities and what each may do, covering authentication and authorization.
  • is the mechanism: a new identity has zero permissions, not even to launch an or create an , until explicitly allowed.
  • Least privilege is the guiding principle: allow only what a person or system needs.
  • Not the same thing: a permission boundary caps the most permissions an identity can hold, and role-based access control ties access to a person's job in the organization.

Which IAM identity when

  • IAM user: one person or application with its own credentials, and AWS advises one per person who needs access.
  • : users who all inherit the group's permissions, ideal when many people need the same baseline access.
  • : an identity someone assumes for temporary permissions, with no long-term username or password.
    • Assuming it swaps your earlier permissions for the role's set.
    • Coffee shop analogy: switching from barista to cashier at midday means changing roles.
    • People, external identities, applications and AWS services can use roles, which also enable federated and cross-account access.
    • Roles are not meant for permanent access.
  • Federation at scale: rather than an IAM user per employee, staff use their corporate login mapped to IAM roles, set up through with .
  • Exam guide update verified 2026-10-09, Manage access keys for IAM users Access keys are long-term credentials, an access key ID plus a access key, that sign programmatic requests to the or , and AWS advises temporary credentials from roles instead and never creating them for the root user.
  • Exam guide update verified 2026-10-09, IAM tutorial: Delegate access across AWS accounts using IAM roles With cross-account IAM roles, users in one AWS account assume a role in another account and get temporary credentials there, so nobody needs a separate IAM user in each account.

IAM policies

  • A policy, written in JSON, holds allow or deny rules for AWS services and resources, scoped as wide as every S3 bucket or as narrow as one.
  • It only takes effect once attached to a user, group or role.
  • Each statement sets an Effect (only Allow or Deny), an Action (any AWS API call) and a Resource (what the call targets).
  • Example: Allow s3:ListBucket on one reports bucket lets a user view that bucket and nothing else.
  • Exam guide update verified 2026-10-09, IAM last accessed information IAM access reports show last accessed information, meaning which services and actions each user, role or policy actually tried to use, so you can remove unused permissions and keep least privilege.
  • Exam guide update verified 2026-10-09, Managed policies and inline policies Custom policies are customer managed or inline policies that you write and change yourself for your own use cases, unlike AWS managed policies, which AWS creates and you cannot edit.

Lessons from the IAM console demo

  • Prefer adding users to a group over attaching policies one by one, since shared permissions then change in one place.
  • AWS managed policies are prebuilt by AWS and reusable, while customer managed policies are your own custom ones.
  • A role can require MFA and carry read-only S3 policies, so it reaches that S3 data and nothing else.

Additional access management services

  • Together these three ease administration and strengthen security, all in support of least privilege.
  • AWS IAM Identity Center centralizes workforce access across AWS accounts and applications.
    • Linked to an existing identity source, it gives staff one login for every connected account and service, which is SSO.
    • This is : one credential set for many applications, services or domains.
    • IAM alone lacks the federation needed to connect an outside identity source.
  • is the central place to store, fetch and rotate secrets such as passwords, database credentials and API keys.
  • shows all your nodes, meaning connection points, across accounts, Regions, multi-cloud and hybrid setups in one view.
    • It reports details like ID and operating system and automates registry changes, user management and security patching.

Visuals

  • IAM labeled graphic: five markers around a diagram where the MFA-protected root user sets up users, groups and roles, each governed by permission policies.
  • Policy statement example (video): a short JSON snippet with its Effect, Action and Resource parts labeled.

Key takeaways

  • Protect the root user with a strong password and MFA, then keep it out of daily work.
  • Default deny is how IAM behaves, and least privilege is the principle for deciding what to allow.
  • Users are individuals, groups share permissions, and roles grant temporary permissions without long-term credentials.
  • A policy defines access only once it is attached to an identity.
  • IAM Identity Center provides workforce SSO by federating with an existing identity source.
  • Secrets Manager centrally manages and rotates credentials and API keys, and Systems Manager oversees and patches nodes.

Scenarios

  • The coffee shop owner who can use every system: the .
  • Extra permissions needed only for a short task: an IAM role.
  • A whole team needs the same baseline access: an IAM group.
  • Defining which S3 bucket people may open: an attached to their identities.
  • Staff should reach AWS with their usual corporate login: IAM Identity Center.
  • Apps need passwords and keys kept and rotated centrally: AWS Secrets Manager.

Terms

  • AWS account root user: The all-powerful owner identity of an AWS account.
  • Multi-factor authentication (MFA): A login needing two or more verification methods.
  • AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM): The service that controls identities and their access.
  • Default deny: IAM's rule that every action is refused until allowed.
  • Principle of least privilege: Granting only the access that is needed.
  • IAM user: An identity for one person or application.
  • IAM group: A set of users sharing the group's permissions.
  • IAM role: An identity assumed for temporary permissions.
  • IAM policy: A JSON document of allow and deny rules attached to identities.
  • AWS managed policy: A prebuilt policy that AWS maintains.
  • Customer managed policy: A policy you write yourself.
  • Federated identity management: One set of credentials for many applications, services or domains.
  • Single sign-on (SSO): One login for every connected account and service.
  • AWS IAM Identity Center: The service for central workforce access and SSO.
  • AWS Secrets Manager: The service that stores, retrieves and rotates secrets.
  • Secret: Private information such as a password, database credential or API key.
  • AWS Systems Manager: The service that centrally manages nodes and automates patching.
  • Node: A connection point in a network, system or structure.

protecting-networks-and-applications.html:
Protecting Networks and Applications

Objectives

  • Explain how a takes an app down.
  • Match each AWS defense to its role.

Notes

DoS versus DDoS

  • A denial of service (DoS) attack exhausts an app's capacity so real customers get no answer.
  • One machine is not enough, so a distributed (DDoS) attack adds many infected computers, or , whose owners have no idea.

UDP flood example

  • Bots ask a helpful public service, like the National Weather Service, for forecasts, forging your address as the sender.
  • Small requests trigger big replies, so your server stalls sorting unwanted data.

Defense built into AWS infrastructure

  • AWS's global footprint of Regions, AZs and edge locations absorbs brute-force attacks automatically.
  • Security groups: virtual firewalls you configure for inbound and outbound traffic, admitting only expected requests, so forecast data on another protocol is dropped.
    • AWS enforces them at network level, so floods meet a Region's capacity, not one instance's.
  • : meets traffic before your frontend server, also at Region level, so it is not swamped.
  • AWS Regions: too big to flood affordably.

Defense through AWS services

  • Using AWS managed services helps: an ELB front door, not an , blunts attacks.
  • Standard: free, automatic, real-time defense against common DDoS attacks, built into ELB, CloudFront and Route 53.
  • AWS Shield Advanced: paid, with in-depth diagnostics and detection and mitigation of sophisticated DDoS attacks, integrating with CloudFront, Route 53 and ELB.
  • Shield plus custom rules can counter complex DDoS attacks.
  • AWS WAF: a web application firewall that refuses requests from IP addresses blocked in its web ACL (web access control list).
    • It also spots bad actors' signatures and uses to catch new threats.
  • Exam guide update verified 2026-10-09, AWS Firewall Manager AWS Firewall Manager centrally configures and enforces firewall rules, such as AWS WAF rules, rules and AWS Network Firewall firewalls, across the accounts in your organization.

Visuals

  • DoS and DDoS timeline: one attacker versus many zombie bots.
  • Infrastructure flashcards: why security groups, ELB and Regions resist floods.

Key takeaways

  • DoS comes from one source, and DDoS from many compromised machines.
  • Security groups and ELB use Region-scale capacity against DDoS.
  • Shield Standard is free and automatic, and Shield Advanced is paid, for sophisticated attacks.
  • AWS WAF blocks listed IP addresses via a web ACL.

Scenarios

  • An EC2 instance as front door: put ELB in front.
  • A web app needs infrastructure DDoS defenses: security groups and ELB.
  • Web requests from IP addresses you blocked: AWS WAF turns them away.

Terms

  • DoS attack: Flooding an app until genuine requests go unanswered.
  • DDoS attack: A DoS attack from many compromised machines.
  • Zombie bots: Infected computers attacking unknowingly.
  • UDP flood: Forging the victim's address so a public service floods it with replies.
  • Security group: A customer-configured virtual firewall for an EC2 instance's inbound and outbound traffic.
  • Elastic Load Balancing (ELB): AWS's managed load balancer, meeting traffic first.
  • AWS Shield: DDoS protection, free in Standard and paid in Advanced.
  • AWS WAF: A web application firewall filtering requests by web ACL.

protecting-data.html:
Protecting Data

Objectives

  • Give an example of data at rest and data in transit.
  • Pick the AWS feature or service that protects data in each state.

Notes

Encryption basics

  • is a lock: only holders of the right key can read data such as customers' phone and card details.
  • One key can lock and unlock, or separate encryption and keys can split the work.
  • At rest: idle data, such as records in a database.
  • In transit: moving data, such as records sent from a database to an app.

Built-in protection for storage

  • AWS offers built-in storage protection plus dedicated protection services.
  • : new buckets have encryption configured, and uploads are encrypted at rest automatically.
  • : volumes and snapshots, boot and data volumes alike, can be encrypted at rest.
  • : all table data is encrypted at rest server-side with keys.

Dedicated data protection services

  • AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS): creates and controls cryptographic keys, the random digit strings that lock and unlock data.
    • You set which users and roles may manage keys and where they are used, keys never leave KMS, and a key can be disabled temporarily.
  • : central management of SSL/ certificates for AWS services and connected on-premises resources.
  • : uses and automation to find and monitor sensitive data at rest in S3, aiding security posture reviews and compliance.

Encryption in transit

  • Example: the coffee shop app sends a phone number between AWS services to text a customer that an order is ready.
  • SSL and its successor TLS use certificates to verify identity, then encrypt the connection.
  • A browser padlock and an address signal an .

Telling similar ideas apart

  • Hashing and salting, used for stored passwords, are one-way and cannot be reversed.
  • Tokenization and masking protect data without keys.
  • A key alone does not secure data in transit, but SSL/TLS does.
  • ACM is for certificates, and AWS KMS for general-purpose encryption keys.
  • and strong passwords protect access, not data in transit.

Visuals

  • Data encryption timeline: lock and key on a customer profile, then at rest versus in transit.
  • Built-in protection flashcards: S3, EBS and DynamoDB .

Key takeaways

  • Only authorized key holders can unlock encrypted data.
  • S3 and DynamoDB encrypt stored data by default, and EBS volumes can be encrypted.
  • AWS KMS creates and controls keys, which never leave it.
  • SSL/TLS certificates encrypt data in transit, and ACM manages them.
  • Amazon Macie uses ML to find sensitive data in S3.

Scenarios

  • Rudy's secret recipe kept in S3: encrypted at rest by default.
  • Controlling who may use the keys that lock your data: AWS KMS.
  • Finding where personal data sits across S3 buckets: Amazon Macie.

Terms

  • Encryption: Making data unreadable without the key.
  • Decryption: Making encrypted data readable again.
  • Encryption at rest: Protecting stored data.
  • Encryption in transit: Protecting moving data.
  • Cryptographic key: A random digit string that encrypts and decrypts.
  • AWS KMS: The service for creating and controlling keys.
  • SSL/TLS certificate: Proof of identity for an encrypted connection, with TLS the newer protocol.
  • HTTPS: Web traffic secured by an SSL/TLS certificate.
  • AWS Certificate Manager (ACM): Central SSL/TLS certificate management.
  • Amazon Macie: ML-based discovery of sensitive data in S3.

detecting-and-responding-to-security-inc.html:
Detecting and Responding to Security Incidents

Objectives

  • Pick the right detection service for a scenario.
  • See how the four services fit together.

Notes

Find weaknesses: Amazon Inspector

  • Prevention can miss unknown software flaws, so detect and react fast.
  • Automatically scans EC2, containers and Lambda for vulnerabilities and best-practice gaps, like open EC2 access or vulnerable software.
  • Ranks findings by severity, each with a fix, in the console or .

Spot threats: Amazon GuardDuty

  • Continuously analyzes account metadata and network activity for threats.
  • Mixes threat intelligence, like known malicious IP addresses, with anomaly detection and ML for accuracy.
  • Lambda can run its fixes automatically.

Investigate: Amazon Detective

  • After detection, it traces the root cause across your accounts.
  • It gathers logs itself, then uses ML and graph analytics to chart resource and user activity over a time window you set, plus fixes.

See it all: AWS Security Hub

  • Pulls findings from AWS and partner services into one format and one view of security and compliance.
  • Sorts them into actionable groups called , and shortens .

Choosing between them

  • Security Hub also shows security data, but for posture and compliance, not deep forensics over time.
  • GuardDuty detects threats but lacks Detective's interactive investigation views.
  • Inspector focuses on vulnerability scanning.

Key takeaways

  • Inspector finds and ranks vulnerabilities.
  • GuardDuty continuously detects threats.
  • Detective visually traces a threat's root cause.
  • Security Hub aggregates findings into one view.

Scenarios

  • Unknown software flaws on EC2: .
  • Suspicious account or network activity: .
  • Tracing how a threat unfolded: .
  • Findings from many services in one view: .

Terms

  • Amazon Inspector: Automated vulnerability assessments.
  • Amazon GuardDuty: Continuous threat detection.
  • Amazon Detective: Visual root cause investigation.
  • AWS Security Hub: One view of all findings.
  • Insights: Security Hub's actionable groups of findings.
  • Time to resolution (TTR): What Security Hub's automated remediation can shorten.

labs.title: Least privilege for the barista
labs.brief: Barista Ana signs in fine but cannot open today's menu files, and the owner wants baristas kept away from deleting menu files and from the payroll export. Switch statements on or off until every case gets its expected result. In this lab, an explicit Deny beats any Allow, and an action that no Allow matches is denied.

Ana deletes the pastry menu file

goals.label: Ana reads the menu and Lee updates it
goals.hint: Ask which single statement gives a barista exactly the read the shift needs, and whether any Deny on the group also reaches that read.

goals.label: Baristas cannot delete menu files or open payroll
goals.hint: Ask how far each Allow reaches, and what a barista may do when no Allow mentions the action or the file at all.

Role-based access control ties access to a person's job rather than stating the need-only rule.
Least privilege is the guiding principle of granting only the access that is needed.

questions.takeaway: An IAM policy grants nothing until it is attached to a user, group or role.

read.text: It only takes effect once attached to a user, group or role.

questions.stem: The cafe wrote a JSON policy that allows listing the reports bucket, yet staff still cannot list it. Which fact about policies explains this?

options.text: A policy has no effect until it is attached
options.why: A policy does nothing until it is attached to a user, group or role, so staff gain nothing yet.

options.text: A policy can hold both Allow and Deny rules
options.why: This is true, but the policy only allows, so mixing rule types does not explain the problem.

options.text: A policy can cover just a single S3 bucket
options.why: This is true, and the policy is scoped to the reports bucket, which is the one staff want to list.

options.text: A policy is written as a JSON document
options.why: This is true of every policy, so it does not explain why this one grants nothing yet.

questions.takeaway: Once identity is proven, authorization uses granted rights to limit what that user can reach.

read.text: Authorization then uses granted rights to limit that identity's actions.

questions.stem: After signing in, a cashier at the cafe can view the day's sales but cannot open the payroll records. Which security idea keeps the payroll records out of the cashier's reach?

options.why: The cashier is already signed in, and granted rights now limit which records they may open.
Authentication already happened at sign-in and only proved who the cashier is.
Encryption encodes stored data but does not decide which signed-in user may open it.
Auditing reviews logs afterward and does not block the cashier from opening records.

labs.title: Which service raised this finding?
labs.brief: The cafe's morning security report lists nine new findings, but the line saying where each one came from got cut off. Sort each finding under the service that raised it.

cards.text: The till server runs a software package with a security flaw attackers could use
The order tracker's EC2 instance is left open to connections from anyone on the internet
The loyalty app's container image carries an outdated package that attackers can exploit
Calls to the cafe account come from an IP address on a list of known attackers
The menu server suddenly sends network traffic unlike anything it sent before
The cafe account shows a burst of activity far outside its normal pattern
An S3 bucket of menu photos also holds a file of customer phone numbers
Customer card details sit in an S3 bucket meant only for sales reports
An S3 export nobody tracked holds loyalty members' names and home addresses

goals.label: Software flaws and weak settings sit under Amazon Inspector
goals.hint: Ask whether the finding is a weakness found by scanning a server, container or function, before anyone attacks it.

goals.label: Suspicious activity sits under Amazon GuardDuty
goals.hint: Ask whether the finding comes from watching account and network activity for known bad actors or unusual behavior.

goals.label: Sensitive stored data sits under Amazon Macie
goals.hint: Ask whether the finding is about personal or payment data resting in S3, rather than about software or traffic.

notes.title: Detecting and Responding to Security Incidents

lines: Amazon Inspector automatically scans EC2, containers and Lambda for vulnerable software and weak settings, and ranks each finding by severity.
Amazon GuardDuty keeps watching account and network activity, using threat intelligence and anomaly detection to spot attacks.
Amazon Macie uses machine learning to find sensitive data, such as phone numbers or card details, stored in S3.

questions.takeaway: Scanning workloads for vulnerable software and ranking the results by severity is the job of Amazon Inspector.

read.text: Automatically scans EC2, containers and Lambda for vulnerabilities and best-practice gaps, like open EC2 access or vulnerable software.

questions.stem: The cafe worries that the EC2 instances behind its till system run software packages with known flaws. It wants those instances checked automatically, with each problem ranked by how serious it is. Which service fits?

options.why: GuardDuty watches account and network activity for threats, not the software installed on the instances.
Inspector scans EC2 instances for vulnerable software and ranks each finding by severity with a fix.
Detective investigates the root cause of an issue after detection rather than scanning for software flaws.
Trusted Advisor checks the account against broad best practices, not each instance's software for known flaws.

questions.takeaway: Ongoing threat detection from account and network activity, including known bad IPs, points to Amazon GuardDuty.

read.text: Continuously analyzes account metadata and network activity for threats.

questions.stem: The cafe wants a service that keeps watching its AWS account and network traffic around the clock. It should raise an alert if, for example, an instance starts talking to an address known to be malicious. Which service fits?

options.why: Inspector scans workloads for vulnerable software rather than watching live account and network activity.
Macie looks for sensitive data stored in Amazon S3, not for suspicious network activity.
GuardDuty continuously analyzes account and network activity and uses threat intelligence such as bad IP lists.
Security Hub collects findings from other services into one view instead of analyzing traffic itself.

questions.takeaway: To find where personal data sits across S3 buckets, use Amazon Macie.

read.text: Amazon Macie: uses machine learning (ML) and automation to find and monitor sensitive data at rest in S3, aiding security posture reviews and compliance.

questions.stem: The cafe has many S3 buckets and is unsure which ones hold customers' personal details. Which service can find and keep watch on that data?

options.why: GuardDuty looks for threats in account activity, not for personal data inside S3 objects.
Macie uses ML and automation to find and monitor sensitive data stored in S3.
Inspector checks workloads for software flaws, not S3 buckets for personal data.
Config tracks resource settings over time, but it does not look inside objects for personal data.

labs.title: Lock the root user
labs.brief: The cafe owner opened the AWS account as the root user, still signs in with it every morning, and once made a root access key for an old billing script. A new manager starts next week, so lock the root user down before then. Set how the root user signs in, which credentials it keeps, and how the team signs in for daily work.

fields.label: Turn on MFA for the root user

options.label: The till password the staff already share
A short word that is easy to remember
Whatever the account password policy allows
options.detail: The account password policy asks for at least 8 characters (a lab value).

options.label: A long password used nowhere else
Keep the existing access key
options.detail: A long-term access key ID and secret access key that sign CLI and API requests.

options.label: Create a new one for the command line
options.detail: A fresh long-term key pair for signing AWS CLI requests.

options.label: The root user
options.detail: The owner identity, which can do anything and cannot be restricted.

options.label: An IAM user for each person, in a group
options.detail: Each person gets their own credentials and inherits the group's permissions.

options.label: AWS IAM Identity Center
options.detail: Staff use one login from an existing identity source, with single sign-on.

goals.label: Root sign-in needs MFA and a strong password of its own
goals.hint: A stolen password alone should not open the owner identity, so ask whether any account-wide rule checks the root password for you.

goals.label: The root user has no access keys
goals.hint: Access keys are long-term credentials that sign CLI and API calls, and AWS advises temporary credentials from roles for programmatic work, so ask what a leaked owner key could do.

goals.label: Daily work happens away from the root user
goals.hint: The owner identity can do anything and cannot be restricted, so ask which identities can carry just the access a day of work needs.

lines: MFA asks for a second kind of proof, such as a one-time code from a phone app, so a leaked root password alone does not open the account.
A password policy sets rules for IAM user passwords only, so the root password has to be strong on its own.
Access keys are long-term credentials, and AWS advises never creating them for the root user and using temporary credentials from roles instead.
The team signs in each day as their own IAM users in a group, or through IAM Identity Center, which maps one login to IAM roles, and the root user stays out of daily work.

questions.takeaway: Even a secured root user stays out of daily work, while IAM identities handle routine tasks.

read.text: Even then, keep the root user out of daily work and use IAM identities instead.

questions.stem: The cafe owner has already given the root user a strong password and turned on MFA. What else does AWS advise for the root user from then on?

options.text: Give it a long and strong password
options.why: AWS does advise a strong password, but the owner has already set one, so it is not the further step.

options.text: Turn on MFA for its sign-in
options.why: AWS does advise MFA for the root user, but the owner has already turned it on.

options.text: Keep it out of daily work
options.why: Even when secured, the root user stays out of everyday tasks, which IAM identities handle instead.

options.text: Cover it with the password policy
options.why: An account password policy sets rules for IAM user passwords only and never applies to the root user.

questions.takeaway: Avoid long-term access keys where you can, never create them for the root user, and prefer role credentials.

read.text: Access keys are long-term credentials, an access key ID plus a secret access key, that sign programmatic requests to the AWS CLI or API, and AWS advises temporary credentials from roles instead and never creating them for the root user.

questions.stem: The cafe owner plans to create access keys for the root user so a nightly script can call AWS. Which fact should change this plan?

options.text: Access keys sign requests to the AWS CLI or API
options.why: This is true and is why the owner wants keys, so it gives no reason to change the plan.

options.text: Each access key pairs an ID with a secret key
options.why: This describes what an access key is made of, not why the root user should not get one.

options.text: Roles give scripts temporary credentials instead
options.why: AWS advises temporary role credentials over long-term access keys, and never keys for the root user.

options.text: AWS Secrets Manager can store and rotate API keys
options.why: Storing root keys in Secrets Manager still leaves long-term root keys, which AWS advises against.

questions.takeaway: An account password policy governs IAM user passwords only, so the root user password needs its own care.

read.text: Password policies set account-wide rules for IAM user passwords, such as minimum length, required character types, expiration and preventing reuse, but they never apply to the root user password.

questions.stem: The cafe just set an account password policy that requires long, complex passwords. Which passwords does that policy govern?

options.text: Database passwords kept in Secrets Manager
options.why: Secrets Manager holds app secrets, and the account password policy only shapes sign-in passwords.

options.text: The root user password for the account
options.why: The password policy never applies to the root user password, which needs its own care.

options.text: IAM user passwords throughout the account
options.why: Password policies set account-wide rules for IAM user passwords.

options.text: One-time codes from MFA phone apps
options.why: MFA codes are generated by a device, and a password policy sets no rules for them.

incidents.title: The developer's missing laptop
incidents.brief: A developer's laptop went missing from the cafe's back office overnight. It held the scripts he runs against the cafe's AWS account and a config file for the order database, and the manager wants the account locked down before the morning rush.

steps.takeaway: Access keys are long-term credentials, so a leaked pair keeps working until someone removes it.

read.text: Access keys are long-term credentials, an access key ID plus a secret access key, that sign programmatic requests to the AWS CLI or API, and AWS advises temporary credentials from roles instead and never creating them for the root user.

steps.stem: The scripts on the missing laptop signed their AWS CLI requests with an access key pair for the developer's IAM user. The manager asks whether she can leave the pair alone and let it lapse by itself. Which fact means she must act on it now?

options.text: Access keys are long-term credentials with no built-in expiry.
options.why: Because the pair is long-term, a copy on the lost laptop keeps signing requests until the manager removes it.

options.text: An access key pair is an access key ID plus a secret access key.
options.why: This describes what makes up the pair, but it says nothing about whether the pair stops working by itself.

options.text: AWS advises never creating access keys for the root user.
options.why: This advice is about the root user, while the lost pair belongs to the developer's IAM user.

options.text: An IAM role grants temporary permissions to whoever assumes it.
options.why: This is true of roles, but the scripts used an access key pair on an IAM user, not a role they assumed.

steps.takeaway: A database password that scripts fetch at run time and that must change on a schedule belongs in AWS Secrets Manager.

read.text: AWS Secrets Manager is the central place to store, fetch and rotate secrets such as passwords, database credentials and API keys.

steps.stem: A config file on the cafe's laptop held the order database password in plain text. The manager wants scripts to fetch that password from one central store each time they run, and wants the password changed on a regular schedule. Which service fits?

options.why: AWS KMS creates and controls the cryptographic keys that lock data, not a store the scripts fetch a password from.
Systems Manager gives one view of nodes and automates patching and user management, not storing and rotating the password.
Secrets Manager stores, fetches and rotates secrets such as database credentials in one central place, as the manager wants.
IAM Identity Center gives staff one sign-in across accounts and apps, and it does not hold or rotate database passwords.

steps.takeaway: IAM access reports show which services and actions an identity actually used, so its unused permissions can be removed.

read.text: IAM access reports show last accessed information, meaning which services and actions each user, role or policy actually tried to use, so you can remove unused permissions and keep least privilege.

steps.stem: Over the years, the developer's IAM user picked up far more permissions than his scripts ever called. Before the user is switched back on, the manager wants to trim it down to the services and actions it has really used. What shows her which permissions to keep?

options.why: A password policy sets rules for IAM user passwords, such as length and reuse, and shows nothing about permission use.
An AWS managed policy is a prebuilt permission set that AWS maintains, and it records nothing about what a user called.
A permission boundary caps the most permissions an identity can hold, but it does not show which ones were used.
An access report shows last accessed information for the user, so she sees what it used and can remove the rest.

incidents.title: The ordering site knocked offline
incidents.brief: On Saturday morning the cafe's ordering site stopped answering customers. Junk requests poured in from a swarm of hijacked home computers, and the manager wants the site back up and much harder to knock over next time.

steps.takeaway: Against a DDoS flood, a managed ELB front door with Region-scale capacity holds up far better than a lone EC2 instance.

read.text: Using AWS managed services helps: an ELB front door, not an EC2 instance, blunts attacks.

steps.stem: The cafe's ordering site takes every request directly on one EC2 instance, so a flood of requests from many machines swamped that single server. Which change makes the site far harder to flood?

options.text: Switch the instance to a larger type
options.why: A larger instance still offers the capacity of one server, which a swarm of bots can still use up.

options.text: Move the instance to another Availability Zone
options.why: In a new zone, the one instance still takes every request on its own, so the flood can swamp it again.

options.text: Put Elastic Load Balancing in front of it
options.why: ELB meets traffic before the server at Region level, so a flood hits AWS-scale capacity instead of one instance.

options.text: Open more ports in its security group
options.why: Opening ports admits more unexpected traffic, while a security group helps by letting in only expected requests.

steps.takeaway: A site behind ELB, CloudFront or Route 53 gets AWS Shield Standard's DDoS defense automatically and at no extra cost.

read.text: AWS Shield Standard: free, automatic, real-time defense against common DDoS attacks, built into ELB, CloudFront and Route 53.

steps.stem: The cafe's ordering site now sits behind Elastic Load Balancing. The cafe skipped every optional protection plan and pays nothing extra for security. Which service is already defending the site against common DDoS attacks?

options.why: Shield Advanced is a paid service the cafe would have to buy, so it is not guarding the site for nothing.
Shield Standard is free, automatic and built into ELB, so it already defends the site against common DDoS attacks.
AWS WAF filters requests only by the rules someone sets up in its web ACL, and the cafe set up no extra protection.
Firewall Manager applies firewall rules that someone configures across an organization's accounts, which the cafe never did.

steps.takeaway: AWS WAF turns away web requests from IP addresses in its web ACL and from bad actors it recognizes by signature.

read.text: AWS WAF: a web application firewall that refuses requests from IP addresses blocked in its web ACL (web access control list).

steps.stem: Some harmful requests still reach the cafe's web app. A few come from IP addresses the cafe has already flagged, and others carry the signatures of known bad actors. The manager wants a filter in front of the app that refuses these requests. Which service fits?

options.why: GuardDuty analyzes account and network activity to detect threats, but it does not sit in front of the app refusing requests.
Inspector scans EC2, containers and Lambda for vulnerabilities, and it does not filter incoming web requests.
Shield Standard automatically absorbs common DDoS floods, but it does not refuse requests by flagged addresses or signatures.
AWS WAF refuses requests from IP addresses blocked in its web ACL and spots bad actors' signatures, as the manager wants.

incidents.title: Loyalty data in a forgotten bucket
incidents.brief: A former analyst exported loyalty data to Amazon S3 for a one-off report and then left the cafe. Nobody knows which buckets the files landed in or what they hold, and the owner wants the data found and locked down before an auditor visits.

steps.takeaway: Amazon Macie's findings on sensitive data in S3 feed the security posture and compliance reviews an auditor looks at.

read.text: Amazon Macie: uses machine learning (ML) and automation to find and monitor sensitive data at rest in S3, aiding security posture reviews and compliance.

steps.stem: Before the auditor visits, the cafe's cloud team turns on Amazon Macie for the cafe's S3 buckets. What does Macie's work give the owner for the compliance review?

options.text: A ranked list of software flaws in the cafe's workloads
options.why: Ranking software flaws in workloads is the job of Amazon Inspector, while Macie looks at the data stored in S3.

options.text: Monitored findings on where sensitive data is stored
options.why: Macie finds and monitors sensitive data in S3, and those findings support security posture reviews and compliance.

options.text: A history of resource settings checked against rules
options.why: Recording resource settings and checking them against rules is the job of AWS Config, not of Macie.

options.text: Alerts on threats seen in account and network activity
options.why: Watching account and network activity for threats is the job of Amazon GuardDuty, not of Macie.

steps.takeaway: Files uploaded to a new S3 bucket are encrypted at rest automatically, with no setup needed.

read.text: Amazon S3: new buckets have encryption configured, and uploads are encrypted at rest automatically.

steps.stem: The analyst created a new S3 bucket for the export and never changed its encryption settings. What protects the files while they sit in that bucket?

options.text: Encryption in transit over an SSL/TLS link
options.why: SSL/TLS protects the files only while they move to or from the bucket, not while they sit in it.

options.text: MFA on the accounts that sign in
options.why: MFA guards who can sign in, and it does nothing to make the stored files themselves unreadable.

options.text: Encryption at rest applied by default
options.why: New S3 buckets have encryption configured, so the uploaded files are encrypted at rest with no setup.

options.text: Hashing and salting, which are one-way
options.why: Hashing is a one-way step used for stored passwords, and S3 does not apply it to uploads, which must stay readable.

steps.takeaway: AWS KMS creates and controls encryption keys, limits which IAM roles use them, never lets them leave and can disable them for a while.

read.text: AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS): creates and controls cryptographic keys, the random digit strings that lock and unlock data.

steps.stem: The owner wants the cafe to control the cryptographic material that locks the loyalty files. Only the finance team's IAM role may use it, it must never leave the service that holds it, and the cafe must be able to switch it off for a while. Which service fits?

options.why: ACM manages SSL/TLS certificates for encrypted connections, not the keys that lock stored files.
AWS KMS creates and controls keys, lets the cafe choose which IAM roles use them, keeps them inside, and can disable one for a while.
Secrets Manager stores and rotates secrets such as passwords, and it does not create and control encryption keys.
Macie finds and monitors sensitive data in S3, and it does not create or control the keys that lock it.
